explanation: Fires on a word-piece beginning with 'ch' (or 'Ch'/'CH', also Cyrillic 'Ч'/'ч') that continues a word after a hyphen, slash, space or prefix: life-changing, co-chromatographed, Editor-in-Chief, tetrachloro, HDL-Cholesterol, ' Challenged'. Other mid-word consonant-cluster pieces like 'ath', 'ech' or 'H' after a hyphen give only weak-to-moderate activation.

Fires on identifier tokens in code or programming discussion that name libraries, packages or classes: Go/JS import path segments (/testify, /pkg, /jquery), product names like Redis, and class-name parts like 'Manager' or 'Driver'. A few plain-English words in programming Q&A (' once', ' statements') fire moderately. Ordinary prose stays near zero.

A mixture of unrelated jobs: the '?
' or ').
' that ends a question right before the answer in math Q&A; the closing '."

' at the end of a quoted statement in news; the '9' in '19xx' years in court headers; plus scattered tokens like license 'following' and 'No you'.

No single pattern. Strong examples include possessives after a family mention ('her son', 'his son', 'my wife'), the opening quote of a nickname, the last digit of a number in math problems, and contrast words like 'latter', 'lower' and 'rural'. It is hard to predict from the token or its context.

Fires on word-pieces in the middle of rare proper names (surnames like Greenblatt, Albrecht, Lamoreaux, Klobuchar, Luxemburg) and of non-English words (German, Danish, Dutch, Portuguese, Hindi), where the word is split into unusual subword fragments. Common English words do not fire.

Fires on prepositions and words of direction, gaze or source that complete a spatial-orientation phrase: 'staring to the', 'coming out of', 'pouring from', 'facing', 'towards', 'in front of', 'look out of'. A related offshoot is 'subject' in the license phrase 'This source file is subject to'. Non-spatial uses of these prepositions are weak.

Fires on subword fragments inside proper names and non-English words, especially in short titles, headers or name lists ('Neuner', 'Zandvoort', 'Lozan', 'Töpel', Greek, Hindi and Japanese pieces), often the second or later piece of the word. English function words and common words are weak.

Fires on the second (completing) token of a fixed multi-token name or compound whose first part strongly predicts it: 'South Sudan', 'Los Angeles', 'University of California', 'Trans-Pacific', 'East Asia', 'micromol/l', 'transfer/copy', 'mobile/cell', 'Aang'. Generic continuations are weak.

Diffuse, with moderate activation on many kinds of token: line breaks and spacing in license and copyright comment headers, clause-introducing words like ' which', ' such', ' where' and ' (', and occasional nouns ('radar systems', 'Arctic Circle'). There is no clear single trigger.

A mixture. It fires on the token that completes a predictable multi-token term or collocation ('opiate withdrawal', 'master's degrees', 'Best Picture', 'arachidonic', 'eigenvectors', 'markitup'). It also fires on digits and pieces of citation and section IDs ('#s005', 'bib0015', 'Cal.App', 'Ill.').

Fires on a preposition or function word right after a verb or noun, where it introduces a following action or complement, often a gerund: 'concluded by', 'responds by', 'protects itself by', 'planning on', 'after averaging', 'chances of', 'on the verge of', 'hard time'. Prepositions introducing plain noun phrases fire less.

Fires at formatting and OCR anomalies: long whitespace runs in court-document headers, gaps where a symbol or number was dropped ('cultivated  of the land', '( )'), OCR misspellings, mojibake, and digits inside numbers in odd formatting. It is a loose mixture of 'garbled or unusual layout' positions.

Two related jobs. (1) The ' [@' that opens the second or later citation in a list of bracketed references ('[@R1], [@R2]'). (2) The first digit after the dash in a year or page range ('1984-85', '1910–13', '1961-1990', 'pages 82-85'). Code-line starts like 'import' and '#include' are weaker.

Fires on arguments inside function signatures or call argument lists in code: parameter names, types and literal values after a comma or opening parenthesis ('b = None', 'innerRadius', 'arg2', ', 0, 0', 'String title'). Digits inside numbers in prose are only moderate-to-weak.

No clear pattern. Strong examples range from a minus sign in math expressions, 'copies' in license text and name endings to many prepositions and nouns ending a comparison or phrase ('superior in', 'alike', 'wild-type mice').

A mixture: method names after modifiers in Java ('boolean equals', 'String toString'); content words in BSD/MIT license boilerplate ('met', 'notice', 'distribution', 'documentation', 'AND'); random-string and base64 pieces; and scattered prose verbs and nouns ('measuring', 'insight', 'calculate').

Fires on highly predictable tokens in document boilerplate and preambles: the first keyword after a license header ('namespace', 'package'), 'www' in the Apache license URL, the '0' in '#sec001' section anchors, 'Code generated by', and 'without published opinion'. Some offshoots: 'has been' in abstracts and digits in years.

Two jobs. (1) The ' (' (or '-') that opens an acronym definition right after a spelled-out multi-word technical term ('vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)'). (2) Package-path pieces in Java/Kotlin import statements and XML namespaces ('import io.', 'org.n|extr|tc', '/student'). Ordinary prepositions are weak.

Fires on verbs of perception or judgment in 'regard/see/view as' frames, especially passive or predicative ones: 'be regarded as', 'be viewed as', 'be seen as', 'is perceived by', 'looked upon', 'treated ... as', 'views'. Literal seeing ('can be seen removing') is moderate.

A mixture: ' so' in 'and so on' or 'and so forth'; the first token after indentation in code blocks (' super', ' console', 'width', ' parent'); library and URL path segments ('/angularjs', 'utm_medium'); and assorted prose words ('made worse', 'related to', 'Marvel').

Fires on the word 'for' as part of a hyphenated compound or identifier ('not-for-profit', 'All-for-Ireland', 'taken-for-granted', 'port-for-deno', '*ngFor', 'idForVideo') and on 'For' at the start of a sentence or quote. The ordinary preposition ' for' inside a sentence gives moderate activation.
